TheReMarkable Paper Prohas everything we like about the ReMarkable 2—a matte screen feels like paper, quick and responsive writing experience, and a great battery life—and adds a few cool new features like colorful pen options and a gentle built-in screen light that uses ambient light from the room. It's got an 11.8-inch screen, making it an extra inch and a half bigger than the ReMarkable 2. It's especially handy if you're taking notes or writing down ideas somewhere a little dark, like a dimmed classroom or on a late flight. Like the ReMarkable 2, it's easy to organize your notes in various ways, from different notebooks to tags and folders. It's easy to access notes off the device, too, especially if you have ReMarkable'sConnect subscription ($4 per month)for unlimited cloud storage. The stylus charges on the device, too.
There are many ways to organize your work into different notebooks or quick sheets, and you can sort them with tags and folders. You also upload PDFs and ebooks to the slate via the company's app or website, and ReMarkable has aChrome extensionthat lets you send any webpage to read on the tablet, and a desktop app that lets you upload PDFs, like a blank Dungeons & Dragons character sheet to fill in on your next game night. You can integrate your notes into Google Drive, Dropbox, or Microsoft OneDrive, though you'll want the Connect subscription for unlimited cloud storage. You can also join the beta program for ReMarkable Methods as a Connect subscriber, which introduces a new library of templates and workbooks you can add to your ReMarkable device. There's also a beta program (that again you'll need to be a subscriber to join) for the new Handwriting Search, which will scan your notes to learn what you've written and allow you to search for it.
The Paper Pro does have its own set of accessories, includingcovers ($179)to protect it and akeyboard folio ($229)if you want to type with it, since it's a different size than the ReMarkable 2. It has its own set of styluses as well, the Marker and Marker Plus—the Marker Plus is a $50 upgrade, but I find the eraser to be well worth it.

Ankle injuries are more common than you think - here's how to protect yours - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesByEmily Holt
They are the body's primary shock absorber, vital for balance, standing, walking and running, but most of us rarely think about our ankles - until we hurt them.
These painful incidents are very common, says Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist who has worked on shows like Strictly Come Dancing.
Ankle injuries account for 5% of visits to A&E in the UK, according toNICE,external.
But Tawiah tellsWhat's Up Docs?they can be avoided "if you are strong and aware of your foot and ankle and the chain that affects it". Here are three ways to strengthen your ankles:

The foundation to building strong ankles and reducing the risk of injuries is being "brain to body aware", says Tawiah - meaning you can sense what movements your ankles are making without relying on looking down at them.
"It's about sending information from the brain down to our foot and ankle to ground us and build a good foundation for any exercise training that follows," she says.
To build brain body awareness Tawiah has some examples of exercises that require you to watch your foot while you do them.
She suggests starting with smaller movements of the toes as this can affect how we "load [weight] through the ankles". Two examples are:
Pressing the tip of your big toe into the floor, holding it and watching how the arch of your foot engages. "This will feel like something pulling through the arch of your foot," she says.
Putting a pen on the floor next to, and parallel with, your big toe. Then try to move the big toe towards the pen, which is called toe "abduction".
How can you better look after your ankles? Listen now.
2. Build strength, control and balance
Tawiah says the function of the ankle is to help us balance, weight bear and transmit force.
Heel raises- Stand next to a sturdy surface and lift your heels off the floor and roll onto your toes, making sure your ankles don't wobble or stick outwards.
Balance- Walk with one foot in front of the other, like a gymnast along a beam, and maintain your foot control.
Control- Moving from a sitting to a standing position on one or two legs and going up or down stairs are also examples of exercises used to improve ankle balance and control.
"If you go up the stairs and you find that you lead with one leg, practice leading with the other side."
Image source,Genevieve TawiahImage caption,
Genevieve Tawiah, a performance physiotherapist, says the foundation to building strong ankles is being "brain to body aware"
Those recovering from ankle sprains might want to try balancing on one leg while throwing and catching a ball. Or work on their landing control by stepping to either side and balancing on the landing leg.
And for those with tendinopathy, chronic pain in the tendon, a slow and heavy load is important. Try calf raises with weight - for instance on a leg press.
Tawiah says picking the right type of shoes is important in supporting your ankles.
"A lot of people fall into the trap of wearing flat ballet pumps, pointy shoes or trainers that are narrower at the front.
"It's just worth imagining if the top of the shoe was off, would your toes have space or would your big toe be pushing over?
"Barefoot shoes are becoming increasingly popular - and can be useful - but it is important to have a good baseline of foot/ankle strength first and pace yourself with using them."
She also recommends looking for "a degree of arch support" as it affects how you take weight through your foot during a task.
She says different activities require different shoes.
"If you're doing squat exercises, you're probably going to want a flatter shoe. If you've got a spongy-soled shoe, it's going to be harder to balance and take the weight in the right place.
"Whereas if you are running, a trainer that provides more cushioning for impact or shock absortion might be more appropriate."
For longer all-terrain walks "hiking boots are often useful in reducing the risk of big sprains. However, wearing them for long periods day to day can cause increased ankle stiffness as it limits ankle mobility to a degree."

Ranking AFC contenders after trade deadline: Who is favorite after Jaguars, Chiefs, Bills make deals? | Sporting NewsSkip to main content
Ranking AFC contenders after trade deadline: Who is favorite after Jaguars, Chiefs, Bills make deals?
Troy Taormina/Imagn Images via Reuters Connect
The AFC playoff picture was pretty well-defined entering the trade deadline, at least in terms of which teams are best positioned to make the cut.
With five teams sitting on two or fewer wins and both theRaidersandRavenson downward trajectories, it's fair to say only nine teams see themselves as firmly in the race right now: the seven teams in playoff spots and theBrownsandTexans, who still have different reasons to believe.
It's entirely possible the seven teams in playoff position through nine weeks are the same seven that make it past the regular season. Among them, who has the advantage?
Here's a look at how each AFC contender stacks up after a busy push to the trade deadline.
MORE:Grading every NFL trade deadline deal
Post-trade deadline AFC contender rankings
TheBillsmight not have the most complete team in the AFC — or maybe they do — but they do have Josh Allen. You might say that hasn't been enough in the past, but we have learned in other sports that droughts are made to be broken and each team should be evaluated on the present rather than the past. In the present, Buffalo has what it takes to win the AFC, particularly with a leg up on the rest of the field for a first-round bye.
Buffalo didn't need to add to its offense at the trade deadline, but the addition of safety Amani Hooker was wise after C.J. Gardner-Johnson's release. The Bills don't want to put Allen in an impossible spot in the playoffs needing every win to come by shootout. After two strong defensive performances and the arrival of Hooker, the Bills have some real hope that the defense will be able to hold serve down the stretch and make this season different.
TheJaguarshave to be considered the Bills' top challenger in the AFC. Jacksonville already had Trevor Lawrence playing some of the best football of his career and a glut of weapons for him to work with. Now, a defense that was more vulnerable made three key additions in Jordan Davis, Jessie Bates and Davon Godchaux.
It's been a more challenging year for Davis, but he and Godchaux fill the void left by the injured DaVon Hamilton while Bates solves a major need at the back end of the defense. The Jaguars were already a top contender before the deadline and came away from it as a better team.
TheChiefshave flaws, but they also have Patrick Mahomes. Andy Reid hasn't had Mahomes play like the Mahomes of the past this season, as the two-time MVP has been limited to shorter throws, but an offense that relies on yards after the catch has really only flopped in one game this season. Kenneth Walker III has added a new dynamic to the offense, and the arrival of Josh Downs at least gives Kansas City another competent pass-catcher.
With Mahomes under center and Steve Spagnuolo's defense always prepared for the stretch run, the Chiefs still have to strike some fear into opponents.
MORE:Chiefs' updated WR depth chart with Josh Downs
TheBroncosare probably comfortable with no one believing in them at this point, but there should be legitimate questions about Denver's ceiling in a more traditional year in which more premier quarterbacks will be in the playoffs out of the AFC.
Denver passed on trading for a running back, meaning the backfield will remain by-committee and keep more pressure on Bo Nix. Can the offense do enough to get by? One advantage the Broncos do have is an AFC West lead, one that could remain intact through the end of the season because the Chiefs have such a difficult stretch of games starting on Thanksgiving.
Sam Greene/The Enquirer/USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images
TheBengalshaven't always passed the eye test this season, and their defense isn't going to intimidate anyone in the playoffs, but they know what works for them: throwing the football. Joe Burrow is playing out of his mind at the moment, and both Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins appear to be healthy and loaded with confidence. As long as that remains the case, Cincinnati can beat anyone.
ThePatriotsare the one current AFC playoff team that could be trouble, especially if the Ravens get themselves together or the Texans make a surge. New England's pass defense caved in against the Packers, and injuries to both wide receivers and running backs have left Drake Maye low on options offensively. Injuries are going to leave the Patriots undermanned against the Lions on Sunday, and a .500 record with seven weeks to go could spell danger for a team that would be one of the AFC's best at full strength.
Are the Steelers really a 6-2 team? Probably not. Pittsburgh has just one win against a team currently in a playoff spot, and most wins have been too close for comfort. The Steelers are going to come back down to Earth unless Mike McCarthy can really get the offense going, but with six wins already on the board, the math certainly works in Pittsburgh's favor when it comes to securing a playoff berth.

In a trade about an hour after the opening bell that involved more than $100 million in options premium, someone exchanged an existing call spread for a more bullish position that captures the next five months of trading in Nvidia.
The core position was the purchase of 52,000 195-strike calls expiring Feb. 19 worth about $57 million – contracts the trader opened for a new long position while simultaneously selling the same number of 245-strike calls for the same expiry, lowering the cost of the trade by $10 million. The net position, a bullish call spread, needs Nvidia to trade above around $206 by expiry, or about 15% higher, to be profitable. If Nvidia stock reaches the short, 245-strike call, it would represent a nearly 40% rally and return the stock to its all-time high of $243, that was reached on October 6th.
The trade was likely part of a "roll" down from an existing 210/255-strike call spread worth about $42 million that was closed out, according to SpotGamma analysis.
"The person got more aggressive rolling this spread down to lower strikes to get more upside exposure by getting higher delta," SpotGamma founder Brent Kochuba said by phone. "They're trading the call spread here because the vol is expensive going into earnings. It's a significant increase in upside delta exposure."
Delta is options parlance for describing how quickly an options price will react to a change in the underlying stock price. The trader's updated position, taken at lower strikes, will make money faster if Nvidia rallies. In other words, it's a higher conviction trade that the chipmaker's stock will soon rebound.
The 195-strike calls they bought for $57 million was the single biggest options trade on the tape Monday, according to SpotGamma. Of the top 20 options trades by dollar-amount, 12 were Nvidia, the data show.
Flows around the stock generally leaned bullish by midday, with 57% of options volume tied to calls and more than $660 million of call premium likely initiated by call-buyers, SpotGamma data show. The most popular single contract by volume was the 180-strike call expiring Monday, that needs Nvidia to recover 1.2% by the bell to break even.

Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 6, 2025.| Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesPart OfNvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next?see all updatesSean Hollister
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers ofa 14,000-person arena absolutely packedwith influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.
Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now.He has left Nvidiaafter seemingly enablingtwo chip smuggling scandalsand allegedly havingthree extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to seeif this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industryand perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely runningthe first $5 trillion company, he wasthevisionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once saidhe preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d workuntil he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies.Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Muskdidn’t exactly found Teslaand has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg hasproven to be neither visionary nor showmanso far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their companydealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always aleatherjacket; anearlierversionwas a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.
His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processingby firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gunto “paint” theMona Lisain one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huangwasa visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward,The Wall Street Journalreportedin 2024.
He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped,The New Yorkerwrotein 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, sellinga million units in just four monthsand paving the way for both the GeForce GPU anda long-term relationshipwith chip fabricator TSMC.
Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone.He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU forotherkinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.”

Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesByTessa WongandOsmond Chia,Reporting fromSingapore
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
Image source,AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption,
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigatedAlice Huang- not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largelyviews China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?NPR's Scott Detrow talks with Dylan Patel of the AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis about Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and whether it opens up the field for Nvidia's competitors.
Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?
November 13, 20264:06 PM ETHeard onAll Things Considered
Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?Listen·5:135:13TranscriptToggle more options
EmbedEmbed<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6040264/nx-s1-10004159" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
NPR's Scott Detrow talks with Dylan Patel of the AI and semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis about Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and whether it opens up the field for Nvidia's competitors.
Nvidia has long been the kingpin of the semiconductor industry, a company whose huge technological bets paid off, making its chips the most in-demand chips in the world and crowning the company, for a time, the most valuable in the world. But with Nvidia's leader, Jensen Huang, out, does that leave an opening for Nvidia's competitors to catch up? We're going to put that question to Dylan Patel. He is founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis, an AI and semiconductor research firm. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.
DYLAN PATEL: Thank you for having me.
DETROW: So you and others have estimated Nvidia is probably a year, two years ahead of its competitors. With Huang out, can other companies catch up?
PATEL: I think that's the biggest risk at least. Over the last, you know, handful of years, Nvidia's lead has actually lessened, and so therefore, they've lost market share, albeit, the market has grown so fast, Nvidia's revenue and profits have skyrocketed so fast. But now, with, you know, many barbarians at the gate, when sort of Jensen is needed most, he sort of is disappearing or (inaudible) the game.
DETROW: Needed most by the company, the industry?
PATEL: I think most - the most to the company. The industry has for a long time tried to roll their own solution, you know, at least as far as the biggest customers. Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon all have been working on their own AI chips for, you know, a number of years. And yet, they all still relied on Nvidia. But their reliance is reducing to some extent, and that's their goal and has been their goal. And now, you know, the only way Nvidia can keep their market share and stay on top of the world is if they out execute everyone - right? - they keep innovating and bringing new technology to the market. But without Jensen, you know, the founder and the visionary of the company, it's going to be a lot harder for them to keep on top.
DETROW: One of the things you've written about that I think is really important to understand is the way that - like, sometimes I feel like a CEO's role in a company is overblown. But how much came to (ph) his personal decisions, his personal decision-making? Let's talk about this first on the supply side. How was his personal relationships with supply chain managers in Korea and Taiwan so key to Nvidia getting what it needed?
PATEL: There's no other company in the supply chain, including in the semiconductor supply chain, where the CEO is, every quarter, meeting with all his suppliers. And, you know, chips are such a complex supply chain. He has hundreds of suppliers. He's talking to every single one of them, going to Korea, going to Taiwan, going to China, meeting, having drinks with them, going to local fried chicken spots, or, you know, night food markets, everything to woo them. And given this is such a complex industry where, you know, products are improving by 2x a year - right? - it's at an incredible pace - you need your suppliers to have full focus and put their best engineers on your product. And this just keeps Nvidia ahead of everyone.
DETROW: I mean, a big part of the reason the company dominated this field the way it did was the really risky big bets that Jensen Huang took. Do you see another CEO taking those bets, or do you see another company trying to establish itself taking the types of bets that he took?
PATEL: You know, there's many visionaries within the company. The challenge is, are there visionaries who are willing to bet the entire company, right? Jensen with CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia what it is, he developed it in 2010, you know, and the company developed it in 2010. And everyone who was a technologist at the time, everyone who was on Wall Street at the time thought it was a waste of money, thought it was a waste of effort. And then it turned out to be the bedrock of all AI software. You know, is someone going to do something that is such a waste of money that, for a decade looks like a terrible bet? It really takes a visionary, and I don't know if too many people will make those kinds of bets. You know, if someone were to ask me, hey, Nvidia without Jensen, a decade from now, are they the one that's bringing the most important new technology to market? I'd probably wager no.
DETROW: Do you have any sense what some of Nvidia's next big bets could be?
PATEL: Yeah, so Nvidia sort of had this history where they started making chips, and then they started making servers, and then they started making systems. Nvidia now is really focused on the end applications. They're making - they're helping companies make medical devices. They're helping companies make satellites. They're helping companies make entire systems that include AI as a part of it. If they don't do this, then most small and medium-sized healthcare companies, and even many of the not - large-but-not-so-largest-ones can't afford to build their own systems out of AI.
And so I think that's where Jensen was heading - right? - was, hey, in automotive, in healthcare, in manufacturing, how do we make it so medium-sized companies, small companies can all start deploying AI throughout their businesses to make them more efficient, increase production, make their products better, make people healthier? Without that, only the biggest companies can do this. And then the profit motive sort of makes it so, you know, all of the profit is captured by a few, not diffused to the whole ecosystem.

fact_units.text: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO | The VergeSkip to main contentThe homepage
Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
The Steve Jobs of GPUs has been shown the door.﻿
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at CES 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada, on January 6, 2025.| Photo by Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty ImagesPart OfNvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned.
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys.
He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.
On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last.

He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers ofa 14,000-person arena absolutely packedwith influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights.

Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now.He has left Nvidiaafter seemingly enablingtwo chip smuggling scandalsand allegedly havingthree extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump.
The world is watching to seeif this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industryand perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it.

That’s because Huang wasn’t merely runningthe first $5 trillion company, he wasthevisionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself.
And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down.
The 63-year-old once saidhe preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d workuntil he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot.
It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies.Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO.
“He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli.
“Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me.
He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago.
It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO.
“He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me.
Elon Muskdidn’t exactly found Teslaand has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg hasproven to be neither visionary nor showmanso far.

Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their companydealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs.
Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own.

Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations.
In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off.
I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform.

(It was not always aleatherjacket; anearlierversionwas a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off.
Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new.
But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage.

He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them.

His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processingby firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gunto “paint” theMona Lisain one shot.
What I didn’t know back then: Huangwasa visionary founder.
He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets.
In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console.
But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward,The Wall Street Journalreportedin 2024.

He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped,The New Yorkerwrotein 2023.
Thankfully, it was a success, sellinga million units in just four monthsand paving the way for both the GeForce GPU anda long-term relationshipwith chip fabricator TSMC.

Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone.He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA.
It was the ability to use a GPU forotherkinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent.
“Originally there was no market or market demand for it.
It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie.

article.title: Công nghệ vợt pickleball: Bước tiến mới từ lõi foam đến sợi carbon
article.summary: Sau ba năm thử nghiệm, thị trường vợt pickleball đang chứng kiến sự chuyển dịch công nghệ đáng kể, với sự xuất hiện của các dòng vợt lõi foam thay thế cho cấu trúc polymer truyền thống.
body: Sự bùng nổ của pickleball trên toàn cầu đã thúc đẩy một cuộc đua công nghệ mạnh mẽ giữa các nhà sản xuất vợt. Sau ba năm liên tục thử nghiệm các dòng sản phẩm mới nhất, giới chuyên môn ghi nhận những bước tiến đáng kể trong thiết kế, đặc biệt là sự thay đổi từ cấu trúc nhựa đúc nhiệt truyền thống sang các loại vật liệu lõi mới.

Điểm nhấn đáng chú ý trong năm 2026 là sự phổ biến của các dòng vợt sử dụng lõi foam kín (closed-cell foam) thay vì lõi polymer dạng tổ ong thông thường. Các mẫu như Diadem Warrior BluCore đang thu hút sự chú ý nhờ khả năng mang lại cảm giác bóng ổn định, độ bền cao và khả năng hấp thụ rung chấn tốt hơn. Theo đánh giá, vật liệu foam không chỉ giúp vợt chịu được các điều kiện nhiệt độ khắc nghiệt mà còn cung cấp sự kiểm soát vượt trội trong các tình huống phòng thủ.

Bên cạnh đó, các dòng vợt truyền thống như Selkirk Vanguard Control Invikta vẫn giữ vững vị thế nhờ sự cân bằng và cảm giác cầm nắm tối ưu. Đối với những người mới bắt đầu, các bộ sản phẩm giá rẻ như Panel Sound vẫn là lựa chọn hợp lý để làm quen với môn thể thao này mà không cần đầu tư quá lớn. Dù công nghệ thermoformed (đúc nhiệt) đang chiếm ưu thế về sức mạnh, sự đa dạng trong lựa chọn lõi foam và sợi carbon aramid đang mở ra những hướng đi mới cho người chơi ở mọi trình độ, từ phong trào đến chuyên nghiệp.

US floats Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership: Zelenskyy | Euronews
ByNathan RennoldsPublished on14 November 2026 - 11:35 GMT+1•Updated11:42ShareCommentsAdd Euronews on GoogleShareFacebookTwitterFlipboardSendRedditLinkedinMessengerTelegramVKBlueskyThreadsWhatsapp
Putin has indicated that Russia will not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and has rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to bring an end to the war continue.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.
"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.
It comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow earlier this week.
During their meeting, Putin signalled that Russia would not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country.
The US envoys later met with Zelenskyy in Ireland on Thursday to discuss ongoing diplomatic efforts, with the trio announcing that, moving forward, Europe would have a "voice" in peace negotiations.
"This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia," Kushner wrote in a post on X.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova appeared to dampen hopes of such an agreement on Friday, saying that as far as her department was aware, "the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."
In further comments shared by the ministry on Friday morning, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov added: "For our part, the position of the Europeans has been comprehensively outlined."
"They are striving by every means possible to join the negotiations, but, as our President has said, they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war," he said.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says - BBC News
Image source,Getty ImagesByAleks Phillips
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump wasable to broker a temporary ceasefirein the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be a small concession in practical terms, but would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

Ukraine is running out of options, and Russia knows it | Russia-Ukraine war | Al Jazeera
Leonid Ragozin is a freelance journalist based in Riga.
Published On 14 Nov 202614 Nov 2026Listen (7 mins)

Add Al Jazeera on GoogleRepresentatives of Ukraine, the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission attend a meeting in Abu Dhabi on November 10, 2026 [Handout/Ukrainian Foreign Intelligence Service via AFP]
The trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States that took place in Abu Dhabi this week may not lead to a rapid breakthrough, but they clearly outline the trajectory of a conflict that might, after all, be nearing its end.
If anything illustrates the political and emotional rift the two sides are yet to bridge, it is President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’sremarks in Copenhagen this week, in which he lamented that Russian leader Vladimir Putin was still alive. Ukraine’s harsh reality, however, is pushing him towards an unsavoury compromise with his arch-enemy.
Kyiv was compelled to enter the talks at the most disadvantageous moment, when it has few means to counter devastating Russian air strikes that damage its key industries and cripple essential infrastructure in major cities. One of Ukraine’s top negotiators, David Arakhamia, who leads Zelenskyy’s parliamentary faction, described the negotiations as among the most difficult he had participated in since 2022. He said the Russians had arrived with very strict instructions and that it had been difficult to soften the tone of the discussions. His assessment confirms that Russia sees itself as well equipped to negotiate from a position of force.
Moscow, meanwhile, expressed optimism about the outcome. Putin’s aide, Vladimir Medinsky, said the talks had brought the two countries closer to peace. Even Arakhamia said there was momentum towards reaching a solution before the end of the year. That optimism, it needs to be noted, comes without any signs of Russia changing its position on the contours of the agreement. Just as it has for years, the Kremlin insists on a genuinely neutral, demilitarised Ukraine which honours the rights of its Russian-speaking population.
If all this comes as a nasty surprise to many in the West, that’s because for most of this year, Western politicians and the mainstream media kept insisting that the tide of war was turning and that Ukraine was getting the upper hand. Their optimism was fuelled by Ukrainian long-range strikes targeting Russian oil refineries as well as by the snail’s pace of Russian advances on the battlefield.
As late as September, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said that “in all but name, Russia has already lost the war”. Around the same time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Russia was not doing well in Ukraine.
When NATO leaders convened for the Ankara summit in July, it seemed that even US President Donald Trump had bought into the idea that Ukraine had the battlefield advantage.
But Russia responded to Ukraine’s surge, backed up by European funds and US intelligence-sharing, with round-the-clock air strikes that are bringing Ukraine close to its pain barrier. Moscow’s message was cruel: any damage Ukraine and the West might inflict on Russia would be met with epic devastation in Ukraine, from which it would take decades to recover.
The coming winter spells nationwide humanitarian disaster. Russian strikes on energy infrastructure have disrupted electricity and central heating supplies. Millions of Ukrainians, particularly in major cities, live in apartment blocks dependent on central heating, without which their homes can become virtually unliveable. Generators can provide temporary power, but their use is making the cost of war enormous for Ukraine and Western taxpayers who fund its war effort.
It is these dire circumstances, rather than pressure from Trump’s administration, that have forced Ukraine to enter the talks. Zelenskyy would have waited at least until the spring had he not felt so pressed.
Ukraine’s surge has failed to shift Moscow’s peace conditions one inch. Meanwhile, the Western perception of this war’s realities has undergone a considerable transformation. There are two major signs of the shifting landscape which directly affect the agenda of the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
For the first time since the start of the war, a larger part of the Western establishment appears to be ready to discuss Europe’s post-war security architecture. The subject was first broached by US negotiator Jared Kushner, causing outrage in the warmongering camp. But Medinsky said after the Abu Dhabi talks that it was the central issue on the agenda.
This topic harks back to the agenda which Moscow brought to the table in December 2021, a few months before the all-out invasion. It did so after the US and Ukraine signed a charter on strategic partnership which may have served as the decisive trigger for Putin’s decision to invade. The very idea of discussing Europe’s security architecture with Moscow became a strict taboo in the West for over four years, but clearly it is not any more.
Curiously, this broad and vital topic was not the main sticking point at the talks, according to Kushner, who said the territorial issue was the hardest. Moscow has long insisted that Ukrainian forces should withdraw from the remaining part of the Donetsk region for talks to succeed.
But Moscow’s opposition to territorial compromise might be an act of deception aimed at achieving maximum gain on overarching geopolitical issues it considers really vital. At the end of the day, it is only propagandist symbolism that prompts the Kremlin to claim Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
The other sign of change is European governments trying to jump on the bandwagon of peace talks even as this exposes a rift between hardliners, like the EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, and pragmatists who believe compromise is unavoidable. The latter most prominently include Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who held a lengthy telephone call with Putin on October 27, ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks, with discreet consent from parts of the EU leadership.

Kallas urged leaders at the EU summit in Dublin to ‘keep the focus’.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenKallas urged leaders at the EU summit in Dublin to ‘keep the focus’.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA
Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
Kaja Kallas says Moscow is trying to divert attention from its aggression by raising issue of European security
The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps thatRussiais setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.
“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”
In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revivedits hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security– demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.
Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia andUkrainehad agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.
European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.
Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.
The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.
Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president, António Costa, said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”
The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.
Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.
But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.
Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”
Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of thecoalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

fact_units.text: US floats Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership: Zelenskyy | Euronews
ByNathan RennoldsPublished on14 November 2026 - 11:35 GMT+1•Updated11:42ShareCommentsAdd Euronews on GoogleShareFacebookTwitterFlipboardSendRedditLinkedinMessengerTelegramVKBlueskyThreadsWhatsapp
Putin has indicated that Russia will not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and has rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Washington had proposed the idea of Ukraine ceding land to Russia in exchange for NATO membership as efforts to bring an end to the war continue.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins NATO?
Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelenskyy told reporters on Friday in comments embargoed until Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.
Zelenskyy added that Ukraine was discussing "specific security guarantees" from NATO and the European Union and that he would ask Ukrainians if they accepted the terms should Western nations confirm.
"I have no right to make that decision on my own," he said.
It comes after Russian President Vladimir Putin met with US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow earlier this week.

During their meeting, Putin signalled that Russia would not back down on territorial demands to control parts of Ukraine and rejected the idea of foreign peacekeeping troops being deployed in the country.
The US envoys later met with Zelenskyy in Ireland on Thursday to discuss ongoing diplomatic efforts, with the trio announcing that, moving forward, Europe would have a "voice" in peace negotiations.
"This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia," Kushner wrote in a post on X.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova appeared to dampen hopes of such an agreement on Friday, saying that as far as her department was aware, "the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."
In further comments shared by the ministry on Friday morning, presidential aide Yuri Ushakov added: "For our part, the position of the Europeans has been comprehensively outlined."
"They are striving by every means possible to join the negotiations, but, as our President has said, they must decide whether they want peace or the continuation of the war," he said.

US has floated Ukraine ceding Donbas for Nato membership, Zelensky says - BBC News
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance as a condition of any peace deal to deter future threats, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow the day prior.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump wasable to broker a temporary ceasefirein the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be a small concession in practical terms, but would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

Floods Force Gaza to Choose Between Clean Water and Pumping Out Sewage | WIREDSkip to main content
As Gaza floodsoverwhelm displacement sites, municipal teams in Al Maghazi refugee camp face a difficult trade-off: Pumping floodwaters out of shelters means taking away fuel needed to supply residents with drinkable water.
“The diesel we use for these pumps comes from the allocation for the wells that are supposed to pump water,” says municipal engineer Imad Abdel Jawad, and this is at a time when their supply is already insufficient.
Rainstorms swept through Gaza over the weekend of November 7 and 8, overwhelming damaged sewage networks and makeshift shelters. In some tents in Al Maghazi, the water was well over a foot deep, Jawad says.
Floodwater covers the ground around makeshift shelters and tents.Photograph: Getty Images
For Hanan Saied, 46, the storm soaked the bedding and clothing she shares with her seven children. She lives in a shelter in Al Maghazi with mud walls, cracks, and plastic sheeting covering the roof, which WIRED Middle East visited.
“The house flooded, and stones and mud fell on us,” Saied says. “The bedding was soaked, and the children’s clothes were soaked.”
Her children used buckets to move water away while her eldest son tried to repair the shelter. Saied spent the night holding her daughter, Sara, who she says has asthma, trying to keep her warm.
Gaza’s Government Media Office has saidat least 70,000tents sheltering displaced Palestinians had flooded within 12 hours.
On 8 November, the Israel account on X, run by Israel’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs,posted, “Contrary to popular belief, Israel does not control the weather.” The post did not explicitly mention Gaza floods.
The flooding comes after widespread destruction of Gaza’s housing. An Aprilassessmentby the European Union, United Nations, and World Bank found that more than 371,888 housing units had been damaged or destroyed and around 1.9 million people internally displaced, often repeatedly.
By 8 November, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)estimatedthat 1.4 million people—65 percent of Gaza’s population—were living in tents or shelters. Humanitarian partners had received appeals from more than 26,000 households whose shelters or belongings had been damaged.
In Al Maghazi, Jawad describes five displacement sites across the camp’s western and northern areas. Parts sit on low ground where rainwater accumulates without an outlet.
His teams used pumps to move water outside the displacement sites. But the problems extend beneath the streets.
Israeli bombardment has damaged sewage manhole covers in Al Maghazi, Jawad says. Other covers have been stolen or deteriorated over time. The resulting openings allow rainwater to pour into sewage networks unable to accommodate the extra volume, causing wastewater to overflow.
“The sewage networks become unable to accommodate the quantities of sewage in addition to the rainwater that leaks into the manholes because the covers are missing,” he says.
Replacement covers are unavailable locally, while materials needed to fabricate alternatives are scarce and expensive. The municipality cannot afford all the work required. Keeping the water supply running takes priority.
“I consider spending money on maintaining wells or maintaining generators to operate water wells a higher priority than allocating some of that money to maintaining sewage manhole covers,” Jawad says.
Floodwater covers the ground around makeshift shelters in Jabalia refugee camp, Northern Gaza Strip.Photograph: Getty Images
These shortages extend across Gaza. In itsNovember 5 report, OCHA said Israeli authorities continued to impose particularly tight restrictions on engine oil, lubricants, spare parts, and new generators. Systems for pumping floodwater and sewage were already failing.
Restoring more sustainable power supplies, the agency added, depended on Israeli permission to import solar panels, reconnect the electricity grid, and restart Gaza’s power plant.
The Israel Defense Forces did not respond to WIRED Middle East’s request for comment on restrictions affecting the entry of equipment and supplies needed for flood prevention and infrastructure repairs.
Jawad says trucks and earth-moving machinery are needed to bring material to displacement sites where water collects on muddy ground, improving conditions beneath and around tents.
The consequences also reach clinics. Dr Asma Saleh, a general practitioner at the Al Maghazi clinic of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), reports an increase in children presenting with respiratory and gastrointestinal illnesses as the rainy season begins.
Saleh says the clinic sees around 120 children daily, including approximately 22 with influenza-like illness diagnosed from symptoms and 13 with gastroenteritis.
“The inhumane living conditions, collapse of infrastructure, the flowing streets contaminated with sewage, and the shortage of medical supplies are all factors that profoundly impact the health care system in Gaza,” she says.
For Saied, the immediate concern is getting Sara through the next storm. Her daughter has more frequent asthma attacks during winter, she says, and the family has neither a nebuliser nor electricity to operate one.
“My older son spent hours repairing our worn shelter using simple tools, but I don’t know what to do during upcoming storms."
This story originally appeared inWIRED Middle East.

Add Al Jazeera on GoogleThe sand embankment that collapsed two days ago on displacement tents in Ard al-Ribat camp, Deir el-Balah, killing four people, including three children [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/ Al Jazeera]ByMaram HumaidPublished On 11 Nov 202611 Nov 2026
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip –Gaza is dealing with the cleanup of catastrophic flooding after storms submerged displacement camps and war-destroyed cities.
Heavy rain has directly affected 106,000 people in Gaza, according to UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged under water and latrines overflowing into camps.

The floods also brought death: a sandbank under pressure from heavy rain collapsed at the Ard al-Ribat displacement camp in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, on Sunday evening, killing three children and a woman.
Without excavation equipment, residents had to dig through the sand with their bare hands to reach people trapped under debris. When darkness came, they used flashlights on their mobile phones to search for survivors.
Zahira al-Sahar, 58, was preparing to sleep in her tent in the camp on Sunday when she and her 28-year-old daughter were almost entombed in the collapse.
“I was lying in my bedding when something suddenly pushed me and came down on top of me,” al-Sahar told Al Jazeera. “The sand reached up to my neck. My daughter was beside me, and she was almost completely buried.”
Her sons came to the rescue. “I told them: ‘Pull your sister out first, then come back for me.’ They pulled her out, then came back and rescued me,” she said.
Meanwhile, in a neighbouring tent, members of the al-Nabhan family were also buried in the sandbank’s collapse.
“[When I realised] I started screaming and calling for people to come and help,” al-Sahar said. “I told everyone that our neighbours had been buried. We kept shouting: ‘Please, save them. Our neighbours are gone.’”
But the family did not respond to the rescuers’ calls. Eight-year-old Salah, his six-year-old sister Maryam, and their mother, Tahrir, 36, who was five months pregnant, were among the dead. Their father, Ahmed, who was only recently released from Israeli detention, is the family’s sole survivor.
Zahira al-Sahar, 58, and her daughter were rescued after being buried beneath sand when an embankment collapsed onto their tent [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/ Al Jazeera]
“[Ahmed al-Nabhan] and his wife had been very happy after he came out of prison. They were looking forward to having another child in a few months,” said Suhaib Abu Darabi, 32, who was among neighbours who rushed to the site to help save them.
Abu Darabi said the collapse sounded like an explosion and was followed by screaming. The site was exposed to the elements and on unstable ground and collapsed after just a few minutes of rain. By the time neighbours reached the area, they found two tents completely buried under debris.
Abu Darabi said residents were digging with whatever tools they could find.
“We managed to clear some of the rubble, but we could not save the people trapped underneath. The scale of the collapse was far beyond what the residents here could handle, given the lack of resources,” Abu Darabi told Al Jazeera.
“The tents that collapsed beneath the embankment are what the world saw. But what people did not see was that all these tents fell to the ground that night. Residents had to repair whatever they could so they could continue living in them.”
In the neighbouring al-Zein family’s tent, four-year-old Habiba was killed, while her mother, Reem, and brother Ibrahim remain in intensive care.
Suhaib Abu Darabi, 32, joined residents attempting to rescue families buried beneath a collapsed embankment [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/ Al Jazeera]
The scale of the damage caused by this winter’s first storm, which began on November 6, was significant and has exposed the dangers faced by families living in tents with little protection from extreme weather.
This is the fourth winter since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, in October 2023, and hundreds of thousands of people are living in tattered tents or makeshift shelters that have been exposed to the elements for years.
More than 26,000 households had reported damage to their shelters or other belongings by November 8, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. The UN estimated that about 1.4 million people, or 65 percent of Gaza’s population, were living in tents or makeshift shelters when the storms hit.
The danger is only compounded by the extensive destruction of Gaza’s infrastructure from Israeli strikes. Drainage networks have been severely damaged, roads and access routes remain in poor condition, and municipalities lack sufficient equipment to remove accumulated rainwater and respond to emergencies.
Gaza’s Government Media Office described the Deir el-Balah sandbank collapse as a humanitarian disaster.
It said it held Israel, the United States administration and the international community responsible and the blocking of proper shelters, construction materials, mobile homes, fuel and spare parts was a factor in the deadly floods.
The media office also said the failure of the so-called Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to act in the crisis also raised “serious questions about the purpose of these bodies”, which have been accused of working with Israel to continue its siege on Gaza.
The Board of Peace said in a statement this week that it had urged Israel to allow essential supplies such as temporary shelters and drainage equipment to enter the enclave.
Aid organisations have also repeatedly called for the entry of shelter materials and equipment needed to repair damaged tents and infrastructure to avoid a repeat of this past week’s deadly events.
Shaima al-Daour, 22, a displaced woman from northern Gaza who works as a nurse in the Ard al-Ribat camp, was also among those who rushed to help the injured.

Gaza Floods Kill 4 - The New York Times
Middle East|Deadly Gaza Floods Reflect Shortfalls of U.S.-Backed Trucehttps://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/world/middleeast/gaza-flooding-israel.html
Aid officials had warned for months that torrential rains in Gaza could turn deadly this winter.
On Sunday, they buried Ahmad Nabhan’s entire family — victims of what President Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza called a “foreseeable” disaster in the crowded enclave.
The United Nations and relief workers had repeatedlysaidthat Gaza’s two million Palestinian residents needed more and better supplies for a winter that many would spend — for the fourth year running — in squalid, trash-ridden camps. Floods, mud and coldhave proved deadlyin years past.
On Sunday night, Mr. Nabhan, 36, stepped out to have coffee with friends in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza. Minutes later, the rains caused a sand embankment to collapse on his tent — burying his wife, Tahrir, 36; his son, Salah, 8; his daughter, Mariam, 5; and his niece Habiba, 4, inside, according tothe Gaza authoritiesand relatives.
“We dug through the sand and rocks, and pulled out their bodies, one by one,” Mr. Nabhan said in a phone interview.
ImageMourners in central Gaza on Monday holding the bodies of children killed in the collapse of a sandbank at a tent camp.Credit...Mahmoud Issa/Reuters
Thousands of other Palestinians lost their shelters and belongings in the weekend storm,according to the United Nations.
The disaster underscored the misery in Gazamore than a yearafter a U.S.-brokered truce ended the warthere between Israel and Hamas.
Mr. Trump’s Board of Peace — which oversees the cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza — issued arare admonishment of Israelfor doing too little to prevent what it called “a foreseeable humanitarian challenge.” On Monday night, the board said that Israel was considering “additional steps,” but that the response “remains insufficient.”
“We call on the leadership of the current government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies,” said the board, which includes several of Mr. Trump’s closest advisers.
Israel hassaidthat it allowed in plenty of supplies, including tens of thousands of tents and blankets, ahead of the winter. And the Israeli military, which oversees aid to Gaza, said many more supplies had been approved but that the United Nations has not yet brought them into the enclave due to logistical and budgetary issues.
ImageA Palestinian man using a shovel to clear muddy water from his tent in Gaza City last week.Credit...Omar Al-Qattaa/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
The cease-fire agreed to last October was supposed not only to end the war in Gaza that Israel launched after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, but also to usher in a new Palestinian administration and pave the way for wide-scale reconstruction. Many Gazans, however, say little has changed for the better.
Israeli forcescontrol at least 60 percent of the Gaza Strip, hemming Palestinians into a crowded pocket near the coast. They have also been bombarding the enclave on a near-daily basis, killing more than 1,600 people since the cease-fire went into effect,according to local health officialswhose tally includes both civilians andHamas combatants.
Hamas militants rule over the vast majority of Palestinians in Gaza. A dozen or so Palestinian technocrats appointed by the Board of Peace to administer the enclave are in Egypt — and wield little influence over affairs inside Gaza.
Hopes that Gaza could soon be rebuilt have dimmed, since Israel has made Hamas laying down its arms a condition for full-scale reconstruction in the enclave. While the Palestinian militantsagreedin July to a U.S.-backed framework for decommissioning and storing weapons, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israelsaidit fell short of genuine disarmament.
In the meantime, many Gazans are living in the rubble of half-destroyed homes or in tents that are dangerously exposed to the elements, according to Pat Griffiths, a spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Jerusalem.
“Palestinians in Gaza desperately need more sustainable, durable shelter options — to keep them safe, to keep them warm,” Mr. Griffiths said. “To have those options, more materials to create those shelters need to be able to enter Gaza.”
Doron Spielman, a spokesman for the Israeli prime minister’s office, said in a statement that Israel had “gone beyond its obligations” to improve the humanitarian situation in Gaza, including by making efforts to improve sanitation and purify water reservoirs.
Mr. Spielman also said that the Israeli government wanted to advance Mr. Trump’s cease-fire plan, but that “Gaza cannot be rebuilt while Hamas remains armed.”
That echoed remarks from Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister, whosaidon Tuesday that “culpability for the distress of Gaza’s residents rests solely with Hamas.”
Mr. Smotrich has previously suggested keeping conditions in Gaza miserable to encourage Gazans to flee the enclave of their own accord. In September, Mr. Smotrich said Israel should try to “take away their hope.”
“If Gaza remains tiny, crowded and destroyed, they will understand they have nothing to do there,” Mr. Smotrich said in atelevision interviewat the time. “They’ll look for places to go.”
Mr. Nabhan says he himself already has lost everything: His hometown of Jabaliya has largely been razed, and now his family is no more.
“When I lost my family,” he said, “I lost my whole world with them.”
Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.
